patient_information: A previously healthy 20-year-old man from southern India. One month before the onset of symptoms, he received five doses of anti-rabies vaccine (purified chick embryo cell vaccine) following a dog bite, but did not receive rabies immunoglobulin (RIG).
history_of_present_illness: The patient had a fever for 4 days, which was followed by tingling and weakness that began in his left leg. Over the subsequent 2 days, the weakness progressed to involve all four limbs, resulting in quadriparesis.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from southern India, a rabies-endemic country. He had a history of a stray dog bite (WHO category III) on his left lower limb one month prior to symptom onset. He received a full course of five active anti-rabies vaccinations but did not receive anti-rabies immunoglobulin as part of his post-exposure prophylaxis.
vitals: On admission, his blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse was 90 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, and his temperature was 38.5°C (101.3°F).
physical_exam: The patient was conscious with normal mental functions (GCS 15/15). Neurological examination revealed a flaccid, areflexic quadriparesis.
labs_and_diagnostics: Blood investigations including serum electrolytes, renal function, and liver function tests were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a protein of 52 mg/dL, glucose of 60 mg/dL, and 340 cells/mm3 (60% polymorphs and 40% lymphocytes). A saliva sample collected at admission was positive for rabies viral RNA by RT-PCR; a CSF sample was negative.
differential_diagnosis: The primary clinical differential was Guillain Barré syndrome, given the rapidly progressive ascending paralysis. Other possibilities considered included post-vaccination encephalomyelitis and other encephalitides such as those caused by arthropod-borne viruses or herpes simplex virus.
management_and_clinical_course: Following admission, the patient developed autonomic instability, evidenced by increased perspiration and significant variability in heart rate and blood pressure. He subsequently developed dysphagia and respiratory distress, requiring mechanical ventilation on the third day of hospitalization. His condition deteriorated, and he died from a sudden cardiac arrest on the fifth day of hospitalization, nine days after the onset of his symptoms.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was paralytic rabies. This was based on the clinical presentation of fever and rapidly progressive flaccid quadriparesis one month after a WHO category III dog bite in a rabies-endemic area. The diagnosis was definitively confirmed by the detection of rabies viral RNA via RT-PCR in a saliva sample. The development of the disease, despite vaccination, was attributed to the omission of rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) from the post-exposure prophylaxis.
